name: Dimmer Switch
tagline: It chops the mains waveform instead of just switching it — which is why the lamp has to match the dimmer.
terminals: Load — dimmed live out to the lamps
Earth — functional earth or plate earth as the design requires
parts: Rotary knob or slider — the control you turn
Rear module — the electronics and the heat sink behind the plate
safety: Match the dimmer to the load. Leading-edge dimmers suit most incandescent and halogen lamps; trailing-edge suits electronic transformers and most LED lamps. A mismatched dimmer buzzes, flickers, will not dim to zero, and can destroy an LED driver. Total load must sit between the dimmer’s minimum and maximum.

points.label: Faceplate
points.detail: A dimmer plate looks like any other, but the unit behind it is deeper and gets warm. Plate and back box both need the depth, and the load rating has to cover the total wattage of every lamp on the circuit.

points.label: Rotary knob
points.detail: Turn to set the level; push to switch on many designs. The knob drives either a potentiometer on older leading-edge units or an encoder on electronic ones — in both cases it is setting the point in each half cycle at which the device switches the load on.

points.label: Fixing screws
points.detail: Two screws into the back box. If the plate sits proud, do not pull it down with the screws: the heat sink needs air behind the plate and a distorted plate can jam the knob.

points.label: Rear module and heat sink
points.detail: The electronics live in the moulding behind the plate and dump their heat through the finned metal body. Dimmers are rated with that heat sink in free air — burying the plate behind curtains or insulating it in a sealed back box derates it and shortens its life.
